# C6. The cross-country test {#esc-oecd26}

Section {{< var p.sec_esc_crossSection >}} of the paper tests the model on the countries of figure
{{< var p.fig_US_OECDdata >}} less Luxembourg, which has no CSES survey. Every country keeps its own workers per
retiree, income distribution, observed design and propensities to vote by income group, from the CSES, and takes from
the U.S. the discount factor $\beta$ and the cost of redistribution as the elasticity $\varepsilon$, so that country
$n$ faces $\lambda_{n,t} = \varepsilon\,\Pi_{n,t}/R_{n,t}$ at its own ratio of the pay-as-you-go return to the market
return. In layer 1 every country also takes the U.S. political weight of the old $\omega$; layer 2 calibrates each
country's $\omega$ to its pension spending at its observed design. The U.S. anchor, where $\omega$ and $\varepsilon$
are calibrated, is measured as every other country is, from the OECD earnings data and its CSES turnout (appendix
{{< var p.app_oecd26_anchor >}} of the paper). This page sets the paper's test beside the same test with every country
voting as the U.S. does.

## The paper's specification {#esc-oecd26-paper}

The paper reports the test in figure {{< var p.fig_OECD26_layer1 >}} and table {{< var p.table_OECD26_slopes >}}, and
each country's political weight and design in layer 2 in table {{< var p.table_OECD26_omega >}}. In the data and in
both layers spending falls with population growth and rises with the Bismarckian index, and the index falls with
population growth, each significantly. The model's spending rises several times as steeply with the index as the
data's, and its index falls less steeply with population growth. Neither spending nor the index is significantly
related to the Gini, in the data or in either layer.

## The U.S. turnout in every country {#esc-oecd26-turnout}

Every country here takes the U.S. propensities to vote by income group, from the CPS, in place of its own, and the
U.S. anchor is calibrated at them, at a lower $\varepsilon$. Luxembourg enters data and model alike, and with it the
data's slopes on population growth are flatter. The relations with population growth and with the index keep their
signs: spending falls with population growth in the data and in both layers and rises with the index, in the model
less steeply than at each country's own turnout but still more steeply than in the data, and the index falls with
population growth in both layers, less steeply than in the data. On the Gini the two turnouts part. At the U.S.
propensities to vote the model's index falls with the Gini in both layers, most steeply in layer 1, where the data
show a rise that is not significant; spending is not significantly related to the Gini in the data or in either layer.

Every country of the paper's test but the U.S. anchor chooses a more Bismarckian design at the U.S. turnout than at its
own, in both layers (table {{< var x.OECD26_Omega_cps >}} against table {{< var p.table_OECD26_omega >}} of the paper),
and the designs are less closely related to the observed ones than at each country's own turnout, in layer 1 barely at
all (appendix {{< var p.app_oecd26 >}} of the paper).

## The countries outside the test {#esc-oecd26-all}

Figure {{< var p.fig_US_OECDdata >}}, and so the test, leaves out the OECD members before 2000 that the model does not
represent. In Korea, Mexico and Turkey a large share of employment is informal, and the model of sections
{{< var p.sec_oecd >}} and {{< var p.sec_esc >}} has no informal households. In Australia, Denmark, Iceland, the
Netherlands and Switzerland funded tiers pay a large share of mandatory benefits, or the public pension is tested
against them, where the model has a single public pay-as-you-go system. [D1](data.qmd) gives the data of the countries
the figure covers.
